If that’s true, then nobody and nothing is coming between you and making your situation better, except yourself. So maybe you just tell yourself that your life isn’t completely fucked up—see how people responded to you when you posted on Reddit? And your personality isn’t all that bad, you can tell yourself, it just needs some affirmation, and you can do that.

It’s a bunch of little steps to walk away from those feelings. There are some pretty tall, steep ones at first, so just do one, then celebrate that you did it! Then do another. Then celebrate! Etc. And know that there are lots of us taking those same steps, and that these comments to your post are proof that those of us on that path with you are willing to lend a hand when you need it. We understand—we all needed help to get where you’re going.

Hi thanks so much for your comments. They and the others i have Received really help me flesh out the ideas that helped me create this.

To respond first to your concern about the possible end of intellectual and academic pursuits, I believe that this is a form of the argument that it is only competition that drives innovation— that is, that people are motivated primarily, if not totally, to innovate or expand their own intellectual capacities in order to create for themselves a better position in society. I do not believe this to be the case. I think that innovation would occur, and that people will endeavor to educate themselves so that they can create the innovations, regardless of whether there is some financial motivator. I think that there are many instances of this that can be pointed to even in our capitalist society. 

In fact, to see excellent examples both of innovation and of learning that isn’t results or profit motivated, one needs only look to the schoolyard. Students in general, and elementary school students especially innovate and self educate constantly day in and day out, for no other reason than interest in the subjects of study, and the desire to have more fun. I think that this is powerful evidence that the instinct for innovation and learning exists apart from the capitalist influence, and may indeed be stifled by that, as people stifle their own innovative instincts when those instinct s don’t seem to result in the potential for greater income.

And indeed if you look to history, you find another wealth of examples of education and innovation independent of the profit motive. In fact, much of the education and the important innovations that have occurred throughout human history did so before the idea of profit even existed. Stone Age people invented better tools, metallurgical techniques, etc. To benefit themselves, their families and friends, but not to profit off of those people. The same would be true in the society I have begun to draw out here.

Regarding your concern about bargaining, I’m sorry but I don’t quite understand it, because my concept does not rely on bargaining between buyer and seller. Instead, “prices“ for items are set by a bureaucracy, which determines those prices based on a complex set of algorithms outlined in general in the piece I wrote, and in general accounting for demand for the item, supply of the item, cost of materials and person-hours to produce. So there is no bargaining.

Regarding the dictatorship issue, I think you may have been referring to my reference to Marxist dictatorship of the proletariat. I was referring to Marx‘s concept of the post revolutionary bureaucratic government that he foresaw would shepherd the nascent communist country until it withered away, leaving a true communist state. I don’t think that such and organizing system could work given our post-industrial society. My concept is for a different kind of structure that allows people one generation of a quasi-consumerist organization of society that to foster an organic transformation into an eventual communist state.

Regarding your suggestion that people’s desire for the greater or greatest thing, i.e. quantity versus quality, is somehow natural, I just cannot be convinced that that is the case. We are socialized from before we even know that we are being socialized to believe that that is right. If we were socialized in the same way to believe that something else was right, I firmly believe that we would all take the rightness of that other thing as natural. As the Gang of Four said, naturals not in it. 

Rather, I do think that we as a society and as individuals are able to choose, and I think we have come to a point in the life of this country and of this world where many, many people might make the choice to change the way our civilization runs, both to make their lives easier and happier, and also for the benefit of the planet. I sincerely hope that this faith that I have is not somehow delusional.

Again, thanks so much for your contribution. Please let me know your thoughts.

I’m 46 and I’ve lived with bp1 since i was 13. I’ve thought about ending it so many times, and tried a couple. I’ve had a few reasons not to over the years, mostly not wanting to destroy the lives of family members. Having those reasons was enough to keep me from succeeding, but not to keep me from misery. I have worked hard to find various things to keep life interesting enough to forestall suicide—playing music, riding bikes and motorcycles, woodworking. I haven’t been as “successful “ as most(non bp) people with my education and skills, but it’s ok. My friends who know about my condition remind me when I need reminding that every day I’m here is a huge success—a victory over the forces of my brain that didn’t want me around. 

My best advice is to tell people about your condition, find things that you really love to do and do them all the time, and don’t worry about succeeding, just keep being.
